newsitem.title: UK: Not enough new aluminium capacity planned - Bird.
newsitem.headline: Not enough new aluminium capacity planned - Bird.

text.p: There is nothing like enough new aluminium capacity in the pipeline both to replace dying smelters and also satisfy demand growth, industry analysts Anthony Bird Associates said.
Its latest annual review of aluminium production costs said average global operating costs at primary smelters in mid-1996 dropped to $1,251 a tonne, delivered, from $1,336 in 1995.

But this was not large in historical terms and the factors behind the lower costs - weak alumina prices, a strong dollar and low electricity costs in some metal linked power contracts - may be shortlived.

The report said that many smelters now at the high end of the cost curve will be hard hit when costs do rise again. By 1998 it suggests that nearly two million tonnes of capacity will be uneconomic at normal metal prices, and will need boom price levels in order to survive.
A further 2.1 million tonnes will be obsolescent and just able to survive at normal metal prices, but not making enough money to secure the future of the plant.
"So 4.1 million tonnes is close to the edge of the cliff," Bird said. "That represents 17 percent of total world capacity and the problem will get rapidly worse from 2000 onwards."

Although aluminium companies have been able to run plants more efficiently when under pressure and achieve impressive reductions in costs "...it's much harder to keep on doing that year after year," Bird said.
Many plants will almost certainly have to close in the medium term and that will have important implications for the rate at which new smelters are being built.
"Right now, the aluminium industry's rate of investment is woeful," "Bird said.
